title: Adopting Principles to Guide Pathways: The Best Model for Geriatric Pain Management
authors: Corey B Simon; Stephanie A. Eucker; Kenneth E. Schmader
pain_condition_detail: chronic pain in older adults, including musculoskeletal pain, neuropathic pain, and pain from multiple chronic conditions
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS as an explanatory framework and intervention rationale, describing it as full integration of biological, psychological, and social components. It does not operationalize BPS into specific variables or measures but uses it to justify a set of clinical principles for geriatric pain management.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that fear leads to avoidance and deconditioning (bio-psych directional), and that expectations influence treatment outcomes (psych-social directional). It advocates for full biopsychosocial integration but does not specify mechanistic pathways linking all three domains.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper advocates for full biopsychosocial integration but primarily elaborates psychological factors, with biological and social factors mentioned but not developed
conceptual_tensions_2: The paper uses BPS language extensively but does not specify how the three domains interact mechanistically
additional_observations_1: The paper is a narrative expert review that proposes clinical principles rather than synthesizing empirical evidence
additional_observations_2: The paper emphasizes patient expectations and therapeutic alliance as key psychological constructs but does not use any standardized instruments
additional_observations_3: The paper references the fear-avoidance model and misdirected problem-solving model but does not test or extend them
synthesis_note: This narrative review uses BPS as an organizing framework for geriatric pain management principles but operationalizes it primarily through psychological constructs (fear, avoidance, expectations, self-efficacy, therapeutic alliance). Biological and social factors are mentioned but not elaborated. Integration is partial: directional links between fear and deconditioning, and between expectations and outcomes, but no triadic mechanism.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used extensively but social domain is thin and integration is partial. Triadic integration is partial because bio-psych and psych-social links are directional but bio-social is only mentioned. Psych-dominant balance reflects the paper's focus on psychological constructs.

citation: Simon et al. (2026), Clinics in geriatric medicine
title: Adopting Principles to Guide Pathways: The Best Model for Geriatric Pain Management
authors: Corey B Simon; Stephanie A. Eucker; Kenneth E. Schmader
pain_condition_detail: Older adults with chronic pain, including back pain, knee osteoarthritis, chronic musculoskeletal pain, and neuropathic pain.
context_note: Older adults in geriatric clinical care; VA rural Veterans and insurance-influenced therapy/surgery pathways are examples.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: Uses BPS as a clinical-management frame: explain pain as multifactorial, guide individualized multimodal care, use expectations/communication/function/movement principles, and justify referrals and pain modulators. It does not define variables or test mechanisms.
integration_mechanism_summary: Pain modulators are proposed to calm pain signaling so patients can move; expectations/social context shape treatment engagement; the Pain-Movement Interface gives a feedback-loop account of movement-evoked pain, activity, participation, and biopsychosocial factors. No explicit mediator/moderator across all three domains is specified.
emergent_labels_12: sensitive and hyperactive pain signaling system
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper rejects the idea that pain is reducible to imaging findings, yet still treats degeneration, arthritis, joints, discs, and neuropathic pain as clinically relevant
conceptual_tensions_2: It rejects linear movement from biomedical to psychological to social, but much of the text still lists domain examples before explaining integration
conceptual_tensions_3: It calls for individualized matching to subgroup responses while also emphasizing that trials and care models are heterogeneous and difficult to compare
conceptual_tensions_4: Pain-modulatory interventions are framed as enabling movement, but efficacy and adverse effects vary across individuals
conceptual_tensions_5: Communication is treated as treatment, but the paper also identifies time pressure, agenda overload, and the need for structured follow-up as barriers
additional_observations_1: The paper is a principles-based expert review rather than a formal guideline or evidence synthesis with quality appraisal
additional_observations_2: BPS is operationalized as clinical principles, not as measured constructs or coded variables
additional_observations_3: The paper explicitly names patient resources/handouts but does not report validated patient-reported outcome measures
additional_observations_4: The only named model with explicit cross-domain feedback language is the Pain-Movement Interface
additional_observations_5: Older adults are treated as a population needing modification of interventions, not as the primary evidence base
additional_observations_6: The article frames communication as a clinical skill and treatment component
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS as a geriatric clinical-management frame rather than an empirical model: it lists domains, prioritizes patient-centered explanation, expectations, communication, function, and movement, and cites pain-modulatory interventions. Social factors are named as context, but the only triadic integration is a broad feedback-loop narrative.
coding_rationale: BPS functions mainly as a clinical organizing/intervention frame. Psychological content dominates; social content is named but thin; triadic integration is descriptive rather than mechanistic.

title: Adopting Principles to Guide Pathways: The Best Model for Geriatric Pain Management
authors: Corey B Simon; Stephanie A. Eucker; Kenneth E. Schmader
context_note: Geriatric pain management in clinical practice settings.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; justification; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS as an explanatory framework for understanding pain complexity in older adults and as an organizing principle for clinical practice, emphasizing integration of biological, psychological, and social factors without specifying mechanistic pathways.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that psychological expectations and beliefs are influenced by social/system factors (insurance, healthcare structure) and in turn affect treatment effectiveness. No biological-psychological or biological-social mechanisms are specified.
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS as integrated framework versus its actual application as primarily psychological with minimal biological integration
conceptual_tensions_2: Ambiguity about how biological factors (e.g., chronic conditions, structural pathology) actually interact with psychological and social factors in older adult pain
additional_observations_1: The paper emphasizes patient-centered communication and expectation management as key BPS applications
additional_observations_2: Function, not pain intensity, is positioned as the primary outcome measure, reflecting a shift in clinical priorities
synthesis_note: This paper uses the biopsychosocial model as an explanatory and organizing framework for geriatric pain management, emphasizing psychological and social factors while minimally addressing biological mechanisms. It proposes integration through expectation formation and healthcare system influences, but lacks mechanistic pathways. The BPS label serves to justify individualized, patient-centered care rather than describe integrated biological-psychological-social mechanisms.
coding_rationale: BPS typology is 'multifactorial' because all three domains are mentioned but psychological domain is elaborated while biological integration is absent. Triadic integration is 'none' as no three-domain mechanisms are specified. Psychological concepts are well-developed with fear-avoidance, expectations, and self-efficacy, while biological factors remain underdeveloped.
